sentences.text: Quetzalcoatlus northropi was one of the largest azhdarchids, a family of toothless pterosaurs characterized by unusually long and rigid necks.
The animal possessed light, hollow bones reinforced internally by struts known as trabeculae, and its skull lacked cranial kinesis, making it essentially a rigid unit.
Quetzalcoatlus is one of the largest flying animals known in history, with recent estimates placing its wingspan at around 10 to 11 meters.

When first discovered, scientists estimated the largest fossils came from an individual with a wingspan of about 15.9 meters, though Douglas Lawson later suggested figures ranging from 11 to 21 meters.
A specific specimen of the related species Q. lawsoni shows three small oval openings on the quadrate bone that may represent puncture wounds.
The genus Quetzalcoatlus was named by Douglas Lawson in 1975.
The first fossils were discovered in 1971 by Douglas A. Lawson during his master's research, consisting of wing fragments found in the Javelina Formation of Texas.
The type species of the genus is Quetzalcoatlus northropi, and the site where the holotype was discovered is approximately 250 miles from the coastline.

Recent research suggests Quetzalcoatlus likely hunted small prey on the ground, similar to storks and ground hornbills. This feeding behavior is known as the terrestrial stalking hypothesis and is common among large azhdarchids.
Douglas Lawson suggested that Quetzalcoatlus was a scavenger similar to vultures, rejecting a piscivorous lifestyle in favor of feeding on carcasses of sauropods like Alamosaurus.

Quetzalcoatlus likely used a pacing gait on the ground, moving limbs on one side simultaneously before switching to the opposite side, and must have been capable of taking off from limited open spaces because no nearby trees or elevations were available for launch.

Quetzalcoatlus northropi likely lived a more solitary lifestyle in a riparian habitat compared to Q. lawsoni, which was abundant in Texas during the Lanciano age in a fauna dominated by Alamosaurus. The Alamosaurus-Quetzalcoatlus association likely represents semi-arid inland plains.
Structures initially thought to be pycnofibres, a type of hair found in some pterosaurs, were later confirmed to be conifer needles.
In 1984, Lev Alexandrovich Nessov erected the subfamily Azhdarchinae to contain Azhdarcho, Quetzalcoatlus, and Titanopteryx.

Quetzalcoatlus lived during the Maastrichtian age of the Late Cretaceous, specifically the Maastrichtian stage between 68 and 66 million years ago in North America. It lived around 67 to 66 million years ago during the latest Maastrichtian.
It is debated whether the species Q. lawsoni should be placed within the genus Quetzalcoatlus. A 2010 study by Mark Witton and colleagues questioned whether Quetzalcoatlus could be validly diagnosed.
